fichas.title: Standard Cross-Sections for Inter-urban Roads
fichas.summary: Standard cross-sections are provided for roads outside built-up areas and should not be deviated from without reason. The appropriate section is selected according to forecast vehicle numbers and road category. The diagrams show standard cross-sections SC 20, SC 15.5, SC 10.5, SC 9.5 and SC 7.5. Cross-sections beside the carriageway also influence the functional and visual structure; footpaths, cycle tracks, stopping and parking, screening, delivery, and commercial areas should be considered.

For roads with adjacent building, there are no standard crosssections. A suitable profile is developed considering the various
requirements of users and adjacent property owners for sections of
the road. The precondition for this is the decision as to which type of
vehicle the road space should be designed for-> p. 391. Examples of
various built-up road cross-sections are given here -> 0- 0.
The intention should be to give the road a distinctive image. This
can be achieved through clear, differentiated dimensions, differing
arrangement of the various cross-sections, a balanced relationship
of the width and height of the street space and diversity of planting.
As a result of this, the layout of the street space should enable
orientation in the street and also in the town itself.

fichas.title: Built-up Road Cross-Section Examples
fichas.summary: Roads with adjacent buildings do not have standard cross-sections; profiles should respond to the needs of road users and adjacent property owners and to the vehicle type intended for the road space. The examples illustrate varied arrangements, including separated pedestrian and cyclist areas, tram and bus facilities, parking, cycleways, and drivable side strips. A distinctive street image can be supported by differentiated dimensions, balanced street width and height, and diverse planting, while enabling orientation.

For roads with adjacent building, there are no standard crosssections. A suitable profile is developed considering the various
requirements of users and adjacent property owners for sections of
the road. The precondition for this is the decision as to which type of
vehicle the road space should be designed for-> p. 391. Examples of

The intention should be to give the road a distinctive image. This
can be achieved through clear, differentiated dimensions, differing
arrangement of the various cross-sections, a balanced relationship
of the width and height of the street space and diversity of planting.
As a result of this, the layout of the street space should enable
orientation in the street and also in the town itself.
